what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat adults who have a genetic condition called Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency (AATD). In this condition, your body does not make enough of a protein that protects your lungs from damage. This medicine helps replace that missing protein and slows down lung damage, especially a lung disease called emphysema. It does not cure the condition, but it helps protect your lungs from getting worse.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an IV infusion (a slow drip into your vein). A healthcare provider, nurse, or trained caregiver will give you this infusion. It is usually given once a week. The infusion is given slowly over a period of about 15 to 30 minutes, depending on the brand. You may receive this at a clinic, infusion center, or at home if trained to do so. Never try to give yourself this medicine unless your doctor and healthcare team have fully trained you and a caregiver on how to do it safely.
dosing: The usual dose is 60 milligrams per kilogram of your body weight, given once every week by IV infusion. Your doctor will calculate the exact dose based on your weight. Do not change your dose on your own. Always follow your doctor's instructions. Each brand may be prepared or given slightly differently, so follow the specific instructions for the brand you are using.
missed_dose: If you miss your weekly infusion, contact your doctor or healthcare team right away to reschedule it as soon as possible. Try to get back on your regular weekly schedule. Do not double your dose to make up for a missed one. Missing doses regularly can reduce how well the medicine protects your lungs, so try your best to keep all scheduled appointments.
storage: Store this medicine in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it in its original packaging and away from direct light. Some brands (like Glassia) can also be stored at room temperature for a limited time — check with your pharmacist or the package instructions for your specific brand. Once the medicine has been prepared (mixed or reconstituted) for your infusion, it should be used right away or within the time frame listed on the label. Do not use the medicine if it looks cloudy, discolored, or has particles floating in it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking. Smoking causes serious additional damage to your lungs and will make your condition much worse, even while on this medicine. Avoid exposure to secondhand smoke as well. Tell your doctor before getting any vaccines, especially live vaccines, as this medicine is made from human plasma and may affect how certain vaccines work. Avoid missing your weekly infusions, as consistent treatment is important for protecting your lungs.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help right away if you experience any of the following during or after your infusion: difficulty breathing or wheezing, chest tightness or pain, sudden dizziness or feeling faint, hives, rash, or itching, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (signs of a serious allergic reaction), fever or chills, nausea or vomiting that is severe, or unusual bruising or bleeding at the infusion site. Also call your doctor if you notice your breathing getting worse over time, or if you develop any signs of infection such as fever, increased cough, or changes in mucus color.
when_it_works: This medicine works from the time of your first infusion to help raise the level of the protective protein in your blood and lungs. However, it works slowly over time to protect your lungs from further damage. You may not feel any immediate or dramatic change in how you feel. The goal of this medicine is to slow the progression of lung damage rather than to provide quick symptom relief. It may take months to years before you notice the benefit of slowing down lung disease. Keep taking it regularly even if you do not feel different.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not fully known how this medicine affects an unborn baby or if it passes into breast milk. Your doctor will weigh the risks and benefits with you. Children: This medicine is approved for use in adults only. It has not been fully studied in children. Older Adults: Older adults can use this medicine, but may need to be watched more carefully during infusions. IgA Deficiency: If you have a condition called IgA deficiency with antibodies against IgA, you should not use this medicine, as it can cause a severe allergic reaction. Make sure your doctor knows your full medical history before starting treatment.
